items.title: [Editorial] Multiple sclerosis: beyond controlling relapses
items.summary: Few neurological diseases have seen a transformation in diagnosis and treatment as remarkable as multiple sclerosis. A chronic, heterogeneous autoimmune condition, it typically begins in early adulthood and affects over 3 million people, with women roughly three times more likely to be affected than men. Characterised by inflammation, demyelination, axonal injury, and neuronal loss, multiple sclerosis can cause relapses and gradual accumulation of disability. Three decades ago, treatment options were few and far between; today, more than 20 disease-modifying therapies are available.

items.title: [Perspectives] What do artists know?
items.summary: Until the day my newborn son died, I worked as an artist. I spent each day in the studio making drawings and films, over 15 years preparing work for exhibitions, commissions, and eventually a doctorate in fine art. After he died (in my arms, peacefully, not unexpectedly), I directed everything I had learned as an artist into writing the story of his birth and death. As it turned out, over those years in the studio I had developed aptitudes well matched to drawing meaning from experience too adverse to bear.

items.title: [Correspondence] Defining success in kidney xenotransplantation
items.summary: Leonardo V Riella and colleagues report the first successful transition from porcine kidney xenotransplantation to allotransplantation.1 The possibility of this bridge raises important questions about its purpose and how its success should be defined—traditionally by graft survival.2 Xenotransplantation could serve different purposes, including reducing time on dialysis for patients waiting for an allograft, decreasing waiting-list mortality, or providing an alternative for patients unlikely to receive an allograft.

items.title: Intraoperative peripheral perfusion index and mortality after noncardiac surgery: a retrospective cohort study
items.summary: Intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring primarily targets arterial pressure and flow but might not adequately reflect tissue perfusion. The peripheral perfusion index provides a continuous, noninvasive, and readily available indicator of peripheral perfusion, but its prognostic significance across surgical populations remains uncertain. We hypothesised that greater intraoperative exposure to low perfusion index would be associated with postoperative complications and mortality.

items.title: Preoperative roxadustat in major elective noncardiac surgery: a phase 2a randomised clinical trial
items.summary: Postoperative complications remain a leading cause of mortality. Experimental data indicate that roxadustat, a first-in-class prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, reduces ischaemia-reperfusion injury, accelerates wound healing, and enhances survival in sepsis. Therefore, preoperative administration of roxadustat might reduce perioperative organ injury. We examined the perioperative tolerability and the potential for adverse surgical interactions with roxadustat.

items.title: Postoperative delirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing: an exploratory cohort study
items.summary: Advanced age is a major risk factor for both delirium and dementia. A potential early biomarker for dementia is the brain-predicted age difference (brainPAD). We hypothesised that brain ageing accelerates after postoperative delirium (POD), and that increased brainPAD is associated with cognitive decline.

items.title: Beyond the binary: vaping and the changing face of perioperative pulmonary risk
items.summary: Postoperative pulmonary complications remain common, and preoperative respiratory risk assessment continues to rely on conventional cigarette smoking status. A recent study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia identifies an association between vaping-related disorder and postoperative pulmonary complications, while showing a less pronounced association with cigarette nicotine dependence. These findings suggest that binary classifications such as smoker and nonsmoker no longer adequately describe inhalational exposure.

items.title: Association of preoperative vaping-related disorder versus cigarette nicotine dependence with postoperative respiratory complications: a multicentre matched cohort study
items.summary: Electronic cigarette aerosols may promote airway inflammation, bronchial hyperreactivity, and impaired mucociliary defence, but their perioperative respiratory safety remains uncertain. We examined whether preoperative vaping-related disorder was associated with a higher risk of postoperative respiratory complications than cigarette nicotine dependence.
